CHIEF COMPLAINT
Nonhealing foot ulcer with recent drainage and redness.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Gregory presents with a nonhealing foot ulcer on his right foot that has been present for approximately two months. He reports that the ulcer recently became red and began draining, which prompted his visit. He believes the ulcer originated from walking barefoot on Dewey Beach. He describes intermittent throbbing pain but denies severe pain; his primary concern is the new onset of drainage and erythema. He has not experienced drainage previously. His PCP recently prescribed antibiotics, which he has not yet filled at the pharmacy but recalls having taken the medication previously, though he cannot recall the specific name.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient reports intermittent throbbing sensation at the ulcer site. Denies fever. No other systemic symptoms reported.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Diabetes mellitus (poorly controlled)

MEDICATIONS
Patient takes diabetes medications but does not consistently check blood sugar. PCP recently prescribed antibiotics (name not recalled by patient; prescription not yet filled).

ALLERGIES
Not documented in this visit.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented in this visit.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works as an ambulance driver. Recently visited Dewey Beach where he sustained the foot injury from walking barefoot.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: normal, afebrile. Foot examination: one by two inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, just proximal to the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint. Erythema and drainage present. Edema noted around the wound. No necrosis visualized. No odor appreciated. No bony exposure noted. Patient reports increased pressure sensation on palpation but denies sharp pain.

RESULTS
Right foot X-ray: No evidence of osteomyelitis. Ankle-brachial index ordered to assess blood supply to the foot.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diabetic foot ulcer with infection of the right foot. Plan includes: (1) Perform debridement to remove dead tissue; (2) Prescribe clindamycin 400 mg orally twice daily for seven days to treat infection; (3) Obtain surgical shoe to reduce pressure on the foot and prevent further irritation; (4) Order ankle-brachial index to determine vascular supply; (5) Follow-up appointment in two weeks for reassessment and possible additional debridement; (6) Patient instructed to call office if any issues arise between visits or if fever or other concerning symptoms develop; refer to urgent care or emergency department if emergency symptoms occur. Patient also counseled regarding need to optimize diabetes control and follow up with PCP to establish comprehensive treatment plan.
